en: Saṃyutta Nikāya 8.1 The Chapter on Vaṅgīsa Sutta 1: The Departure At Sāvatthī. There, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, when a noble disciple has emerged from the home life into homelessness, he does not think: ‘I have departed from my mother,’ or ‘I have departed from my father,’ or ‘I have departed from my brother,’ or ‘I have departed from my sister,’ or ‘I have departed from my wife,’ or ‘I have departed from my children,’ or ‘I have departed from my slaves,’ or ‘I have departed from my workers,’ or ‘I have departed from my servants. Rather, having emerged from the home life into homelessness, he thinks: ‘I have departed from birth, aging, and death; I have departed from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; I have departed from suffering, I say. When a noble disciple has emerged from the home life into homelessness, he does not think: ‘I have departed from my mother,’ or ‘I have departed from my father,’ or ‘I have departed from my brother,’ or ‘I have departed from my sister,’ or ‘I have departed from my wife,’ or ‘I have departed from my children,’ or ‘I have departed from my slaves,’ or ‘I have departed from my workers,’ or ‘I have departed from my servants. Rather, having emerged from the home life into homelessness, he thinks: ‘I have departed from birth, aging, and death; I have departed from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; I have departed from suffering, I say. This, bhikkhus, is called a noble disciple who has truly emerged, who has truly gone forth, who has truly become a renunciant. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Elated, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words. (This concludes the first sutta in the Chapter on Vaṅgīsa.)
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Venerable Vaṅgīsa was dwelling at Āḷavī at the Aggāḷava Shrine together with his preceptor, the Venerable Nigrodhakappa.
Now at that time, the Venerable Vaṅgīsa was a novice, having recently gone forth, and was left behind as the guardian of the monastery.
Then a number of women, having adorned themselves, approached the Aggāḷava Monastery to look at the dwellings.
When the Venerable Vaṅgīsa saw those women, dissatisfaction arose in him, and lust disturbed his mind.
Then it occurred to the Venerable Vaṅgīsa:
“It is a loss for me indeed, it is no gain for me;

it is ill-gained by me indeed, it is not well-gained by me, that dissatisfaction has arisen in me and lust corrupts my mind. How could it be possible here for another to dispel my dissatisfaction and arouse delight in me?
Suppose I were to dispel my own dissatisfaction and arouse delight in myself.”
Then the Venerable Vaṅgīsa, having dispelled his own discontent and generated delight, on that occasion spoke these verses:
“Alas, though I have gone forth from the home life into homelessness, while I am still dwelling in peace...”
Thoughts run wild;
these are the audacious ones from the dark side,
like high-born sons of great archers.
Trained and wielding firm bows,
they would surround him on all sides—
a thousand who do not flee.
Even if more women than these should come here,
they will not cause me any distress.
It is firmly established in the Dhamma.
For I have heard this directly from the Buddha,
the Kinsman of the Sun, as my own witness.
The path leading to Nibbāna—
therein my mind delights.
While I am dwelling thus,
“Evil One, you come to me;
I shall deal with Death in such a way that you will not see even my path.”

Vaṅgīsa-vagga Arati-sutta (The Discourse on Discontent) At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, discontent is a defilement of the mind; negligence is a defilement of the mind; lack of clear comprehension is a defilement of the mind; and association with people who are unwholesome is a defilement of the mind. When this was said, the Venerable Vaṅgīsa said to the Blessed One: “Discontent is a defilement of the mind, Negligence is a defilement of the mind, Lack of clear comprehension is a defilement of the mind, And association with people who are unwholesome is a defilement of the mind. But when one has abandoned discontent, And negligence, and lack of clear comprehension, And has avoided association with people who are unwholesome— Such a person is called ‘one who has removed the defilements. “Good, good, Vaṅgīsa! On one occasion... [as before] ...the Venerable Vaṅgīsa was dwelling at Āḷavī at the Aggāḷava Shrine together with his preceptor, the Venerable Nigrodhakappa.
Now on that occasion, after returning from his alms round following the meal, the Venerable Nigrodhakappa would enter his dwelling in the evening or emerge from it the next day at the proper time.
At that time, however, dissatisfaction had arisen in the Venerable Vaṅgīsa, and lust corrupted his mind.
Then it occurred to the Venerable Vaṅgīsa:
"It is a loss for me, truly not a gain for me;

it is ill-gotten for me, truly not well-gotten for me, that dissatisfaction has arisen in me and lust corrupts my mind. How could it be possible here that another might dispel my dissatisfaction and arouse delight in me?"
"What if I were to dispel my own discontent and arouse delight by myself?
Then the Venerable Vaṅgīsa, having dispelled his own discontent and aroused delight by himself, at that time spoke these verses:
"Having abandoned both discontent and delight..."
Completely abandoning thoughts associated with the household life,
he should not create any thicket of craving anywhere;
for such a one, delighting in Nibbāna and free from attachment, is indeed a bhikkhu.
Whatever here on earth or in the air,
whatever form exists within the world—
all that decays; all is impermanent.
Thus, having understood this, those who are liberated conduct themselves.
Yet people remain attached to acquisitions—
what is seen, heard, sensed, and known.
Dispel desire for this;
one who is unshaken and does not cling here is called a sage.
Now, those sixty [states] associated with thought...
Various unrighteous views have taken root among the multitude;
yet that monk does not side with any faction anywhere, nor does he speak anything that is coarse or wicked.
Dabba, long concentrated,
free from guile, wise, and without envy,
the sage has attained the peaceful state by depending [on the teaching].
“Having attained final Nibbāna, he awaits his time.
— *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 8.3 (SN 8.3, SN 211, PTS [1st ed. SN i 187; PTS [2nd ed.
SN i 403) 1. The Chapter on Vaṅgīsa
The Pesalasutta.
On one occasion the Venerable Vaṅgīsa was dwelling at Āḷavī at the Aggāḷava Shrine together with his preceptor, the Venerable Nigrodhakappa.
Now on that occasion the Venerable Vaṅgīsa, on account of his own inspired eloquence, looked down upon other bhikkhus who were skillful.
Then it occurred to the Venerable Vaṅgīsa:
"It is a loss for me, truly not a gain for me; it is ill-gained by me, truly not well-gained by me, that I, through my own inspired eloquence, should hold other amiable bhikkhus in contempt."
Then the Venerable Vaṅgīsa, having himself aroused remorse within himself, at that time spoke these verses:
“Abandon conceit, Gotama,
and abandon the path of conceit;”
For a long time, having been utterly consumed by the path of conceit and filled with remorse,
people have been defiled by hypocrisy.
Struck down by pride, people fall into hell;
struck down by pride and reborn in hell, they grieve for a long time.
For the bhikkhu who has conquered the path and practices rightly never grieves;
he enjoys both renown and happiness.
They call him "one who sees the Dhamma," one who is resolute in self-exertion.
Therefore, being unblemished here, striving,
and having abandoned the hindrances, he is purified.
Having abandoned conceit without remainder,
the one who has made an end through clear knowledge is a peaceful sage.
1. The Chapter on Vaṅgīsa:
The Discourse to Ānanda.
At one time the Venerable Ānanda was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then, in the morning, the Venerable Ānanda dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Sāvatthī for alms with the Venerable Vaṅgīsa as his attendant monk.
Now at that time, dissatisfaction had arisen in the Venerable Vaṅgīsa, and lust assailed his mind.
Then the Venerable Vaṅgīsa addressed the Venerable Ānanda in verse:
“I am burning with sensual desire;
my mind is consumed by fire.
Please tell me how to achieve its extinguishing.”
“Out of compassion for you, O Gotama.
“Because of a perversion of perception,
your mind burns with fever.”
Avoid the sign associated with beauty and lust;
view conditioned phenomena as alien.
Do not regard it as self or as suffering;
extinguish your great passion,
lest you burn again and again.
Develop the mind through the meditation on foulness,
one-pointed and well-concentrated;
let mindfulness directed to the body be established within you.
Abound in disenchantment;
cultivate the signless and abandon the underlying tendency to conceit.
Then, through the full realization of conceit, you will live in peace.
—Saṁyutta Nikāya 8.5 (SN 8.5, SN 213, PTS 1st ed. SN i 188; PTS 2nd ed. SN i 406)
1. The Chapter on Vaṅgīsa, Discourse on Well-Spoken Words.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus.
“Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, speech endowed with four factors is well-spoken, not ill-spoken; it is blameless and beyond reproach to the wise.
With which four?

“Here, monks, a monk speaks only what is well-spoken, not what is ill-spoken; he speaks only the Dhamma, not what is non-Dhamma; he speaks only what is pleasing, not what is displeasing; he speaks only the truth, not what is false.
It is by being endowed with these four factors, monks, that speech is well-spoken, not ill-spoken, and is blameless and beyond reproach to the wise.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, further spoke these words:
"The virtuous say that well-spoken speech is supreme;
one should speak the Dhamma, not what is not-Dhamma—this is the second."
“One should speak what is pleasing, not what is displeasing; that is the third.
One should speak the truth, not falsehood; that is the fourth.
Then the Venerable Vaṅgīsa rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, extended his joined palms in reverential salutation toward the Blessed One, and said this to the Blessed One:
“It occurs to me, Blessed One; it occurs to me, Sugata.
“Let it occur to you, Vaṅgīsa,” the Blessed One said.
Then the Venerable Vaṅgīsa praised the Blessed One to his face with appropriate verses:
One should speak only that speech which does not burn oneself and does not harm others.
That indeed is well-spoken speech:
one should speak only pleasant words,
those words which are welcomed in return.
That which, without taking up evil,
one speaks as pleasant to others—
truth indeed is the nectar-like word.
This is the eternal Dhamma;
the virtuous say that the good are established in truth, in the goal, and in the Dhamma.
Whatever word the Buddha speaks for the attainment of Nibbāna,
for the bringing about of the end of suffering—
“That indeed is the supreme among words.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 8.6 (SN 8.6, SN 214, PTS [1st ed. SN i 189, PTS [2nd ed.
SN i 408) 1. Vaṅgīsa-vagga
The Sāriputta Discourse.
On one occasion the Venerable Sāriputta was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.

Now on that occasion the Venerable Sāriputta was instructing, urging, rousing, and gladdening the bhikkhus with a talk on the Dhamma—speech that was polished, clear, articulate, expressive of the meaning.
Those bhikkhus listened to the Dhamma with attention, with their minds directed toward it, with all their hearts, and with ears inclined.
Then it occurred to the Venerable Vaṅgīsa:

“This Venerable Sāriputta is instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening the bhikkhus with a discourse on the Dhamma, using speech that is polished, clear, flawless, and expressive of the meaning.”
Those monks listened to the Dhamma with intent, paying close attention, applying their whole minds, and lending an ear.
"What if I were to praise the Venerable Sāriputta to his face with appropriate verses?
Then the Venerable Vaṅgīsa rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, extended his joined palms toward the Venerable Sāriputta, and said this to him:
“It occurs to me, friend Sāriputta; it occurs to me, friend Sāriputta.
“Let it occur to you, friend Vaṅgīsa.
Then the Venerable Vaṅgīsa praised the Venerable Sāriputta to his face with appropriate verses:
“Of profound wisdom and intelligent,
skilled in what is the path and what is not the path,
Sāriputta is of great wisdom.”
He teaches the Dhamma to the bhikkhus;
he teaches it in brief and speaks upon it in detail.
Like the song of a sālika bird,
he uttered a inspired response;
as he was teaching that, [the assembly]...
They hear a sweet voice,
with a tone that is enchanting,
worthy of being heard, and melodious.
“With uplifted minds and joyful, the bhikkhus lend their ears.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 8.7 (SN 8.7, SN 215, PTS [1st ed. SN i 190, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 410)
1. The Chapter on Vaṅgīsa: The Discourse on the Invitation.

At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Park, in the Mansion of Migāra’s Mother, together with a great Saṅgha of monks, about five hundred monks in all, who were all arahants.
Now at that time, on the Uposatha day of the fifteenth, the Blessed One was seated in the open air surrounded by the community of monks for the Pavāraṇā ceremony.
Then the Blessed One, having surveyed the silent community of monks, addressed the monks:
"Come now, monks, let me invite you."
"And do not find anything to criticize in me, whether it be physical or verbal.

When this was said, the Venerable Sāriputta rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, extended his joined palms in reverential salutation toward the Blessed One, and said to the Blessed One:
"Indeed, Bhante, we do not criticize the Blessed One for anything, whether physical or verbal."

For the Blessed One, venerable sir, is the arouser of the unarisen path, the producer of the unproduced path, the declarer of the undeclared path; he is the knower of the path, the discoverer of the path, the one skilled in the path.
And now, venerable sir, the disciples dwell following that path, having subsequently attained it;
and I too, venerable sir, invite the Blessed One [to point out any fault].
“Nor does the Blessed One reproach me for anything, whether bodily or verbal.
“I do not reproach you for anything, Sāriputta, whether bodily or verbal.
You are wise, Sāriputta; you are one of great wisdom, Sāriputta; you are one of broad wisdom, Sāriputta; you are one of laughing wisdom.”
"Sāriputta, you have fleet intelligence; Sāriputta, you have sharp intelligence; Sāriputta, you have penetrative intelligence.

Just as, Sāriputta, the eldest son of a wheel-turning monarch correctly continues the wheel set in motion by his father, even so, Sāriputta, you have correctly continued the unsurpassed wheel of Dhamma set in motion by me."
“If it is true, Bhante, that the Blessed One does not reproach me for anything,
whether bodily or verbal, then why, Bhante, does the Blessed One not reproach these five hundred bhikkhus for anything,
whether bodily or verbal? “Sāriputta, I do not reproach even these five hundred bhikkhus for anything, whether bodily or verbal.”

“Sāriputta, of these five hundred bhikkhus, sixty bhikkhus are possessors of the three knowledges, sixty bhikkhus are possessors of the six direct knowledges, sixty bhikkhus are liberated both ways, and the rest are liberated by wisdom.
Then the Venerable Vaṅgīsa rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, extended his joined palms in reverential salutation toward the Blessed One, and said to the Blessed One:
“It occurs to me, Blessed One; it occurs to me, Sugata.”
“Let it occur to you, Vaṅgīsa,” the Blessed One said.
Then the Venerable Vaṅgīsa praised the Blessed One to his face with these appropriate verses:
“Today is the fifteenth, the day of purification.”
Five hundred bhikkhus have assembled together;
these seers have severed the bonds of the fetters,
are free from distress, and have exhausted all further becoming.
Just as a wheel-turning monarch,
surrounded by his ministers,
Traverses all around [his realm].
This earth bounded by the ocean—
thus [I praise] the unsurpassed Caravan Leader who has conquered the battle.
The disciples, possessors of the threefold knowledge who have abandoned death, attend upon him;
they are all the sons of the Blessed One.
No falsehood is found here;
I pay homage to the Kinsman of the Sun, the slayer of the arrow of craving.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 8.8 (SN 8.8, SN 216, PTS [1st ed. SN i 192, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 414) 1. Vaṅgīsa-vagga Parosahassa-sutta (More than a Thousand) At Sāvatthī. There, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are more than a thousand bhikkhus here who are arahants with taints destroyed, who have lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, reached their own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and are liberated through final knowledge. Just as, bhikkhus, in this Jambudīpa there are many great rivers—such as the Ganges, the Yamunā, the Aciravatī, the Sarabhū, and the Mahī—which flow toward the ocean; even so, bhikkhus, there are more than a thousand bhikkhus here who are arahants with taints destroyed... and are liberated through final knowledge. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, bhikkhus! “Friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Ānanda. The Venerable Ānanda said this: “Friends, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How the Blessed One has taught the Dhamma by way of the simile of the great rivers. For, friends, just as in this Jambudīpa there are many great rivers—such as the Ganges, the Yamunā, the Aciravatī, the Sarabhū, and the Mahī—which flow toward the ocean; even so, friends, there are more than a thousand bhikkhus here who are arahants with taints destroyed... and are liberated through final knowledge. But, friends, how many bhikkhus are there who are arahants with taints destroyed... and are liberated through final knowledge? “Friend Ānanda, we do not know how many bhikkhus are arahants with taints destroyed... and are liberated through final knowledge. But, friend Ānanda, we know that there are more than a thousand bhikkhus here who are arahants with taints destroyed... and are liberated through final knowledge. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and reported everything that had occurred, adding: “It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would clarify the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it. “This, Ānanda, is not the first time that I have taught the Dhamma by way of the simile of the great rivers. It was also taught by me in the past. Ānanda, in the past, when King Mahāsudassana was ruling the kingdom of Kusāvatī, he had a park called Subhaga. There, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana used to go to the park with his harem. And there, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana’s chief queen, Queen Subhaddā, used to give birth to twin sons every year. When the eldest son, Prince Pāyāsi, was twenty years old, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana had six thousand sons, all of whom were brave, heroic, and capable of withstanding an army. Then, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana addressed Prince Pāyāsi: ‘Come, prince, take charge of the kingdom. ‘I cannot, father,’ Prince Pāyāsi replied. ‘I am fond of the religious life, father; I wish to lead the holy life under the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. A second time... a third time, King Mahāsudassana addressed Prince Pāyāsi: ‘Come, prince, take charge of the kingdom. A second time... a third time, Prince Pāyāsi replied: ‘I cannot, father; I am fond of the religious life, father; I wish to lead the holy life under the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Then, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana summoned his ministers and said: ‘Come, ministers, take charge of the kingdom for my son, Prince Pāyāsi. ‘As you command, sire,’ those ministers replied to King Mahāsudassana. Then, Ānanda, Prince Pāyāsi went to the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, instructed, urged, roused, and gladdened Prince Pāyāsi with a talk on the Dhamma. Then, having been instructed, urged, roused, and gladdened by the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, Prince Pāyāsi requested the going-forth from the household life into homelessness. Then, Ānanda, the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, gave the going-forth to Prince Pāyāsi, and the higher ordination. Not long after his higher ordination, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, the Venerable Pāyāsi, by realizing it for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life entered and dwelt in that unsurpassed goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness. He directly knew: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being. And the Venerable Pāyāsi became one of the arahants. Then, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana addressed his ministers: ‘Come, ministers, bring Prince Pāyāsi here. I wish to see Prince Pāyāsi.

‘Sire, Prince Pāyāsi has gone forth from the household life into homelessness under the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery, together with a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus, with twelve hundred and fifty bhikkhus.
Now on that occasion the Blessed One was instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening the bhikkhus with a Dhamma talk concerning Nibbāna.
And those bhikkhus were listening to the Dhamma with eager ears, attending to it as a matter of vital concern, and applying their whole mind to it.
Then it occurred to the Venerable Vaṅgīsa:
"The Blessed One is instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening the bhikkhus with a Dhamma talk connected with Nibbāna.
And those bhikkhus are listening to the Dhamma, having applied their bones, having applied their minds, attending with their whole heart, and lending an attentive ear."
“What if I were to praise the Blessed One to his face with appropriate verses?
Then the Venerable Vaṅgīsa rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One, and said to him:
“It occurs to me, Blessed One; it occurs to me, Sugata.”
“Let it occur to you, Vaṅgīsa,” the Blessed One said.
Then the Venerable Vaṅgīsa praised the Blessed One to his face with these appropriate verses:
“More than a thousand bhikkhus...”
He attends upon the Sugata as he teaches the stainless Dhamma,
Nibbāna, which is free from fear from every quarter.
They hear the stainless Dhamma taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One;
truly, the Sambuddha shines forth.
Honored by the community of monks,
the Blessed One is named Nāga,
the seventh sage among sages.
Having become like a great cloud,
he rains down upon his disciples;
having emerged from his midday rest, he showers them with the Dhamma.
"Out of a desire to see the Teacher,
O Great Hero, the disciple Vaṅgīsa pays homage at your feet."
“Vaṅgīsa, were these verses previously reflected upon by you, or did they occur to you spontaneously?
“Venerable sir, these verses were not previously reflected upon by me; rather, they occurred to me spontaneously.
“In that case, Vaṅgīsa, let even more verses, never before reflected upon, occur to you spontaneously.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Vaṅgīsa replied to the Blessed One, and with even greater measure he praised the Blessed One with verses never before considered:
“Having overcome Māra’s path of the wrong way,
you wander about, having shattered all obstructions.”
Behold him, the one who brings release from bondage,
the Unattached One, dividing [the world] into its constituent parts,
for the sake of crossing over the flood.
He has proclaimed the manifold path;
and those who see the Dhamma stand firm and unshakable in that which has been proclaimed as the Deathless.
Having penetrated through and become a light-maker,
he saw the transcendence of all standpoints;
having known and realized it, [he taught].
He taught the foremost among the tenfold [teachings].
When the Dhamma is thus well-taught,

"Therefore, indeed, in the teaching of that Blessed One, one should always train diligently, paying homage.

1. The Chapter on Vaṅgīsa:
The Discourse to Koṇḍañña.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Then the Venerable Aññāsikoṇḍañña, after a very long time, approached the Blessed One; having approached,
he prostrated with his head at the Blessed One’s feet, kissed the Blessed One’s feet with his mouth,
stroked them with his hands, and announced his name:
“I am Koṇḍañña, Blessed One! I am Koṇḍañña, Sugata!
Then it occurred to the Venerable Vaṅgīsa:
“This Venerable Aññāsikoṇḍañña has approached the Blessed One after a very long time; having approached...”
Having prostrated with his head at the Blessed One’s feet, he kissed the Blessed One’s feet with his mouth, stroked them with his hands, and announced his name:
“I am Koṇḍañña, Blessed One; I am Koṇḍañña, Sugata.”
"What if I were to praise the Venerable Aññāsikoṇḍañña in the presence of the Blessed One with suitable verses?
Then the Venerable Vaṅgīsa rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One, and said to the Blessed One:
"It occurs to me, Blessed One; it occurs to me, Sugata."
“Let it occur to you, Vaṅgīsa,” the Blessed One said.
Then the Venerable Vaṅgīsa praised the Venerable Aññāsikoṇḍañña in the presence of the Blessed One with these appropriate verses:
“That elder was enlightened after the Buddha;”
Koṇḍañña is one of fierce exertion;
he is a frequent attainer of blissful dwellings and of seclusions.
Whatever is to be attained by a disciple who acts according to the Teacher’s instruction—
all that has been attained by him.
For one who trains with diligence,
there is great power: he becomes possessed of the three knowledges and skilled in discerning the minds of others.
“Koṇḍañña, the heir of the Buddha, pays homage at the feet of the Teacher.

1. The Chapter on Vaṅgīsa:
The Discourse to Moggallāna.

On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on the Black Rock on the slopes of Mount Isigili together with a great Saṅgha of monks, about five hundred monks in all, all of whom were arahants.
The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna examined their minds with his own mind and found them liberated and free from acquisitions.
Then, it occurred to the Venerable Vaṅgīsa:
“The Blessed One is staying here at Rājagaha on the Black Rock on the slope of Mount Isigili, together with a great Saṅgha of bhikkhus, about five hundred bhikkhus, all of whom are arahants.”
“The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna has indeed examined their minds with his own mind and found them liberated and free from acquisitions.
What if I were to praise the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna in the presence of the Blessed One with appropriate verses?
Then the Venerable Vaṅgīsa rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One, and said this to the Blessed One:
“It occurs to me, Blessed One; it occurs to me, Sugata.
“Let it occur to you, Vaṅgīsa,” the Blessed One said.
Then the Venerable Vaṅgīsa praised the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna in the presence of the Blessed One with these appropriate verses:
“Sitting on the slope of the mountain,
the Sage who has gone beyond suffering—
his disciples attend upon him.”
Possessing the threefold knowledge,
having abandoned death— Moggallāna, of great psychic power, surveys them with his mind.
The minds of those who have attained it are completely liberated and free from acquisitions.
Thus, endowed with all factors,
They attend upon Gotama, the Sage who has gone beyond suffering and is endowed with manifold qualities.”

Saṃyutta Nikāya 8.11 (SN 8.11, SN 219, PTS [1st ed. SN i 195, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 420) 1. Vaṅgīsa-vagga Gaggarā Sutta At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Campā on the banks of the Gaggarā Lotus Pond. Then the Venerable Vaṅgīsa approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Vaṅgīsa recited these verses in the presence of the Blessed One: “Having seen the Dhamma, having understood the Dhamma, having penetrated the Dhamma, having crossed over doubt, being free from perplexity, having attained fearlessness, and having become independent of others in the Teacher’s Dispensation—such a person is called ‘one who has seen the Dhamma. “Just as a man with good eyesight, standing on the bank of a pond, sees a lotus that is blue, large, and blooming, with its stalk and all; so too, when a bhikkhu knows himself as he really is, he is called ‘one who has seen the Dhamma. “Just as a man with good eyesight, standing on the bank of a pond, sees a lotus that is red, large, and blooming, with its stalk and all; so too, when a bhikkhu knows himself as he really is, he is called ‘one who has seen the Dhamma. “Just as a man with good eyesight, standing on the bank of a pond, sees a lotus that is white, large, and blooming, with its stalk and all; so too, when a bhikkhu knows himself as he really is, he is called ‘one who has seen the Dhamma. When this was said, the Blessed One told the Venerable Vaṅgīsa: “Excellent, Vaṅgīsa! Excellent, Vaṅgīsa! It is well said by you, Vaṅgīsa, when you say: ‘Having seen the Dhamma, having understood the Dhamma, having penetrated the Dhamma, having crossed over doubt, being free from perplexity, having attained fearlessness, and having become independent of others in the Teacher’s Dispensation—such a person is called “one who has seen the Dhamma. “Just as a man with good eyesight, standing on the bank of a pond, sees a lotus that is blue, large, and blooming, with its stalk and all; so too, when a bhikkhu knows himself as he really is, he is called ‘one who has seen the Dhamma. “Just as a man with good eyesight, standing on the bank of a pond, sees a lotus that is red, large, and blooming, with its stalk and all; so too, when a bhikkhu knows himself as he really is, he is called ‘one who has seen the Dhamma. “Just as a man with good eyesight, standing on the bank of a pond, sees a lotus that is white, large, and blooming, with its stalk and all; so too, when a bhikkhu knows himself as he really is, he is called ‘one who has seen the Dhamma. Then the Venerable Vaṅgīsa, having been praised and commended by the Blessed One, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is amazing, venerable sir! How well the Venerable Vaṅgīsa spoke these verses in the presence of the Blessed One! “It is because he had cultivated that state, Ānanda, it is because he had developed that state, it is because he had made that state his vehicle, it is because he had made that state his foundation, that the Venerable Vaṅgīsa was able to speak thus in my presence. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, the Venerable Ānanda delighted in the Blessed One’s words. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir! those bhikkhus replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is possessed of five qualities, he is capable of quickly understanding the Dhamma taught by the Tathāgata. What five? Here, a bhikkhu is possessed of faith, possessed of virtue, possessed of learning, possessed of energy, and possessed of wisdom. When a bhikkhu is possessed of these five qualities, he is capable of quickly understanding the Dhamma taught by the Tathāgata. This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Sublime One rose from his seat and went to his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had gone, a certain bhikkhu approached the Venerable Ānanda, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said to that bhikkhu: “Friend, did you hear the discourse the Blessed One gave just now? “Yes, venerable sir. “What did you understand, friend, was the meaning of that discourse? “Venerable sir, I understood the meaning of that discourse exactly as the Venerable Ānanda explained it to me. “It is good, friend. It is good, friend. For the meaning of that discourse is exactly as the Venerable Ānanda explained it to you. On one occasion the Venerable Vaṅgīsa was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now on that occasion, not long after having attained arahantship, the Venerable Vaṅgīsa, experiencing the bliss of liberation, spoke these verses at that time:
“Formerly we wandered about, intoxicated by poetry;”
From village to village, from city to city,
we then beheld the Perfectly Enlightened One,
and faith arose within us.
Thus he taught me the Dhamma:
the aggregates, the sense bases, and the elements.
Having heard his Dhamma, I—
I went forth into the homeless life.
For the benefit of many indeed,
the Sage attained enlightenment.
To the monks and to the nuns who see that they have entered the fixed course of rightness:
"Welcome indeed has been my arrival!"
In the presence of my Buddha,
the three types of higher knowledge have been attained;
the teaching of the Buddha has been accomplished.
I know my former abodes;
the divine eye has been purified;
I am possessed of the threefold knowledge and have attained supernormal powers.
“Skilled in the penetration of the minds of others.
Its summary verse is:
“Departed, and indeed, aversion...”
The verses on not despising the virtuous;
the well-spoken words of Ānanda;
and Sāriputta’s invitation to question.
More than a thousand [verses] by Koṇḍañña,
by Moggallāna at Gaggarā,
and twelve by Vaṅgīsa.
The Saṃyutta on Vaṅgīsa is complete.
